principle: Choose services from requirements: latency, throughput, consistency, durability, availability, compliance, operational effort, and cost. Popularity is not a requirement.
answer_format: Because the requirement is X, I choose A over B. The request flows through these steps. The main tradeoff is this. I would secure it with that, and validate it by measuring this.
source_note: Condensed from your SAA-C03 quick reference and rewritten for speaking practice. Verify current Region availability, quotas, and pricing before a real design.

tables.title: Compute and hosting

rows.use: You need OS or runtime control, legacy software, custom agents, or special instance types.
rows.tradeoff: You patch and manage capacity.

rows.use: Short event or API handlers that scale automatically and bill per request.
rows.tradeoff: 15-minute limit, concurrency limits, stateless execution, cold starts.

rows.use: AWS-native container scheduling with simple AWS integration.
rows.tradeoff: AWS-specific orchestration model.

rows.use: Kubernetes APIs, ecosystem, or portability is a requirement.
rows.tradeoff: More platform and cluster work.

rows.use: Run ECS or EKS tasks without managing worker nodes.
rows.tradeoff: Less host control; compare cost for steady, high utilization.

rows.use: Deploy a common web app with little infrastructure setup.
rows.tradeoff: Less flexible than your own infrastructure as code.

rows.use: Queued, large-scale batch jobs.
rows.tradeoff: Built for jobs, not low-latency requests.

tables.rule: EC2 when control matters, Lambda when the work is event-driven and bounded, ECS for AWS-native containers, EKS when Kubernetes is a requirement.

tables.title: Storage and transfer

rows.use: Objects: static assets, backups, logs, data lakes, media.
rows.tradeoff: Not a mounted disk; design keys, lifecycle rules, and bucket policies.

rows.use: Low-latency block storage for one EC2 instance: boot and data volumes.
rows.tradeoff: Lives in one AZ; plan snapshots for recovery.

rows.use: Shared NFS file system for many Linux clients.
rows.tradeoff: Network file latency and cost; not a block volume.

rows.use: Managed Windows (SMB), Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, or OpenZFS.
rows.tradeoff: Pick by protocol, performance, and app compatibility.

rows.use: On-premises apps reach AWS storage as file, volume, or tape.
rows.tradeoff: Hybrid operations and cache sizing still matter.

rows.use: Online bulk transfer between on-premises and AWS storage.
rows.tradeoff: Limited by your network bandwidth.

rows.use: Huge offline transfers or edge compute with poor connectivity.
rows.tradeoff: Shipping lead time; not a network.

rows.use: Long-term archive at low storage cost.
rows.tradeoff: Retrieval time and cost vary by class.

tables.rule: Object, block, or file is the first decision. For large migrations compare the network, DataSync, and Snow on time and cost.

tables.title: Databases

rows.use: Managed relational engines for SQL, transactions, and existing schemas.
rows.tradeoff: A Multi-AZ instance standby serves no reads; use read replicas or a cache to scale reads.

rows.use: MySQL or PostgreSQL compatible with faster failover, up to 15 replicas, Global Database.
rows.tradeoff: Validate engine compatibility and cost.

rows.use: Key-value or document data with predictable low latency at any scale.
rows.tradeoff: Model access patterns and keys first; no ad hoc joins.

rows.use: Hot reads, sessions, computed results in memory.
rows.tradeoff: Invalidation, memory sizing, and app changes.

rows.use: Analytical SQL over large data: warehouse and BI.
rows.tradeoff: Not a transactional database.

rows.use: Full-text search and log exploration.
rows.tradeoff: Index design and cluster operations.

rows.use: Timestamped measurements and time-series queries.
rows.tradeoff: Check current options: Timestream for LiveAnalytics closed to new customers in 2025; evaluate Timestream for InfluxDB.

tables.rule: RDS or Aurora for relational transactions, DynamoDB when access patterns are known, Redshift for analytics, and a cache only when the workload benefits.

tables.title: Networking and edge

rows.use: Network boundary with public and private placement.
rows.tradeoff: Plan CIDRs, routes, AZ spread, and egress.

rows.use: Stateful allow rules on resources.
rows.tradeoff: Deny inbound by default; reference other security groups.

rows.use: Stateless allow and deny at the subnet.
rows.tradeoff: Return traffic needs explicit rules.

rows.use: HTTP and HTTPS routing by host and path.
rows.tradeoff: Layer 7; the default for web and API traffic.

rows.use: Very high throughput TCP, UDP, TLS, and static IPs.
rows.tradeoff: Layer 4; less application-aware routing.

rows.use: DNS records, health checks, routing policies.
rows.tradeoff: DNS failover is only as good as the target you fail over to.

rows.use: Cache and accelerate content at the edge.
rows.tradeoff: Cache keys, TTLs, invalidation, and origin access control.

rows.use: Private instances start outbound IPv4 connections.
rows.tradeoff: Not an entry point; one per AZ for resilience; data processing cost.

rows.use: Encrypted tunnel over the internet, or a dedicated private link.
rows.tradeoff: Direct Connect is not encrypted by default; add VPN or MACsec.

rows.use: Reach a service privately without the public internet.
rows.tradeoff: Plan endpoint policies and DNS.

tables.rule: Typical public web tier: Route 53, CloudFront with WAF, ALB, then app servers in private subnets. Databases stay private.

tables.title: Identity, security and governance

rows.use: Temporary, scoped permissions for people and workloads.
rows.tradeoff: Least privilege; no long-lived keys in code.

rows.use: Workforce SSO with permission sets across accounts.
rows.tradeoff: Centralize people; workloads still use roles.

rows.use: Create and control encryption keys.
rows.tradeoff: Key policy and IAM policy both decide access.

rows.use: Store, fetch, and rotate credentials.
rows.tradeoff: Fetch at runtime; never bake secrets into images.

rows.use: Free TLS certificates for integrated services.
rows.tradeoff: CloudFront needs the certificate in us-east-1.

rows.use: Filter HTTP requests with managed and custom rules.
rows.tradeoff: Attach to CloudFront, ALB, or API Gateway.

rows.use: DDoS protection; Advanced adds response support.
rows.tradeoff: Layer with architecture, WAF, and runbooks.

rows.use: Managed threat detection from account telemetry.
rows.tradeoff: Findings need triage and automated response.

rows.use: Who called which API, when, from where.
rows.tradeoff: Organization trail into a locked-down central bucket.

rows.use: Configuration history and compliance rules.
rows.tradeoff: Detects drift; remediation must be wired up.

tables.rule: IAM roles, private networking, encryption, central logs, and least privilege are defaults, not add-ons.

tables.title: Messaging, events and orchestration

rows.use: Durable work queue: consumers poll, spikes are buffered, retries are independent.
rows.tradeoff: Standard is at least once; make consumers idempotent and add a DLQ. FIFO adds ordering and a 5-minute dedupe window.

rows.use: Push one message to many subscribers.
rows.tradeoff: Pair with SQS so each consumer keeps its own backlog.

rows.use: Route events by pattern or schedule to many targets.
rows.tradeoff: Plan retries, DLQ, and archive and replay.

rows.use: High-volume ordered stream with replay within retention.
rows.tradeoff: Plan shards and consumer throughput.

rows.use: Managed near-real-time delivery to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch.
rows.tradeoff: Buffers records; not instant.

rows.use: Multi-step workflows with retries, branches, and human waits.
rows.tradeoff: Keep each task small; the workflow holds state.

rows.use: Managed REST, HTTP, and WebSocket entry point.
rows.tradeoff: Configure auth, throttling, validation, and logging.

rows.use: Apps that already speak ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ.
rows.tradeoff: Good for migration; less elastic than SQS and SNS.

tables.rule: Queue distributes work, topic fans out, event bus routes, stream keeps order and replay, workflow holds state.

tables.title: Data, analytics and AI

rows.use: Object lake plus table and schema metadata.
rows.tradeoff: Partition and use columnar formats to control scan cost.

rows.use: Serverless SQL directly over S3.
rows.tradeoff: Pay per byte scanned: Parquet, compression, partitions.

rows.use: Scheduled or serverless data preparation.
rows.tradeoff: Test transformations and schema changes.

rows.use: Central warehouse for repeated BI queries.
rows.tradeoff: Keep analytics off the transactional database.

rows.use: Dashboards and BI.
rows.tradeoff: Serve curated, permissioned datasets.

rows.use: Build, train, tune, deploy, monitor custom models.
rows.tradeoff: Only when you need custom model control.

rows.use: Generative AI apps on hosted foundation models.
rows.tradeoff: Add retrieval, Guardrails, evaluation, and data access controls.

rows.use: Task-specific managed AI: documents, speech, images.
rows.tradeoff: Prefer these when they meet the requirement.

tables.rule: Data lake: land raw data in S3, catalog and transform with Glue, query with Athena, and serve curated data through Redshift or QuickSight.

tables.title: Resilience, monitoring and IaC

rows.use: High availability across independent AZs.
rows.tradeoff: Not regional disaster recovery.

rows.use: Recover from deletion or corruption.
rows.tradeoff: Define retention, immutability, RPO, and test restores.

rows.use: Copy data to another Region.
rows.tradeoff: Replication is not a tested failover plan, and it copies corruption too.

rows.use: Rising readiness, cost, and complexity.
rows.tradeoff: Choose by RTO, RPO, and business impact.

rows.use: Metrics, logs, dashboards, alarms.
rows.tradeoff: Alert on service-level indicators people can act on.

rows.use: Patching, inventory, run commands, automation runbooks.
rows.tradeoff: Role-based access and change control.

rows.use: Repeatable infrastructure as code.
rows.tradeoff: Version templates, review change sets, separate environments.

rows.use: Central backup policies across services.
rows.tradeoff: Copy across accounts and Regions; rehearse restores.

tables.rule: Resilience is end to end: compute, data, identity, DNS, secrets, quotas, deployment, and runbooks must all meet the recovery objective.

scenarios.title: Highly available web application
scenarios.scenario: A public web app with variable traffic, private application servers, a relational database, and static assets.

steps.text: Route 53 resolves the hostname; the client connects to CloudFront over HTTPS.
CloudFront serves cached static files from S3 and forwards dynamic requests to the ALB. WAF filters bad requests at the edge.
The ALB sends traffic to healthy app targets across AZs; Auto Scaling adds or removes capacity.
The app uses its IAM role to read database credentials from Secrets Manager, then queries the private database over TLS.
CloudWatch metrics, logs, and alarms drive scaling and incident response.

why.reason: HTTP routing by host and path. Use NLB for Layer 4, extreme throughput, or static IPs.
Fails over automatically. Add read replicas or a cache if reads need to scale.
Static files never touch the app servers.

scenarios.watch: Keep the app and database private. Production also needs CI/CD, backups, WAF rules, encryption, health checks, and a tested failover.

scenarios.title: Video-on-demand streaming
scenarios.scenario: Accept video uploads, transcode them into streaming formats, store the output durably, and deliver it worldwide with low latency.

steps.text: The client uploads straight to S3 with a presigned URL; the app records metadata through an API.
The S3 object-created event goes through EventBridge to SQS, which buffers and retries transcode jobs.
MediaConvert writes adaptive-bitrate renditions, manifests, and segments to the output bucket.
CloudFront pulls from the private bucket through origin access control and caches segments near viewers.
Use IAM roles, encryption, lifecycle rules, and job-failure alarms; signed URLs or cookies for paid content.

why.reason: Durable object storage suits media files and segment delivery.
Absorbs upload bursts and separates upload from transcoding.
Lower latency for viewers and far less load on the origin.

scenarios.watch: This is on demand. Live streaming needs live ingest and packaging, such as MediaLive and MediaPackage, and different latency choices.

scenarios.title: IoT telemetry and alerts
scenarios.scenario: Ingest device telemetry securely, process the stream, store current and historical measurements, and alert on thresholds.

steps.text: Devices authenticate to AWS IoT Core with X.509 certificates and publish over MQTT with TLS.
IoT rules send messages to Kinesis Data Streams for real-time consumers and to Firehose for a durable raw archive in S3.
Lambda validates and enriches each record, writes measurements to the time-series store, and publishes threshold alerts to SNS.
Dashboards query curated data; the S3 history feeds batch analytics with Glue and Athena.
Apply per-device policies, least privilege, retries with a DLQ, and monitoring.

why.reason: Device identity, MQTT connectivity, and rules in one service.
Streams for custom consumers and replay; Firehose for managed delivery.
A time-series database for range queries over time; DynamoDB for current device state by key.

scenarios.watch: Define device identity lifecycle, offline buffering, message size and rate, retention, and ordering before sizing the stream. Check current time-series options: Timestream for LiveAnalytics closed to new customers in 2025.

scenarios.title: AI and ML inference application
scenarios.scenario: Expose a model through an authenticated API, optionally ground answers in company documents, and monitor quality and cost.

steps.text: The client calls API Gateway over HTTPS; a Cognito or IAM authorizer checks identity.
Lambda or ECS validates input, applies business rules, and calls the model with a scoped IAM role.
For RAG, retrieve only the chunks this user may see, then call Bedrock and return a grounded answer with citations.
Store only the request metadata and feedback you need; watch latency, errors, model behavior, and token cost.
Redact logs, evaluate outputs, apply Guardrails, and set timeouts and a fallback.

why.reason: Hosted foundation models, no model servers to run.
When you train or host a custom model on a managed endpoint.
Lambda for short API work; ECS for long-running or streaming responses.

scenarios.watch: Managed AI does not remove the need for data authorization, evaluation, prompt-injection defenses, human review of high-impact decisions, and cost controls.

scenarios.title: Containers and microservices
scenarios.scenario: Run independently deployable services with controlled ingress, service-to-service calls, image delivery, and observability.

steps.text: CI builds and tests the image, then pushes an immutable tag to ECR.
ECS or EKS deploys tasks across AZs: Fargate to skip node management, EC2 nodes for more control.
The ALB or API Gateway exposes approved routes; services talk privately through internal endpoints and scoped security groups.
Each service owns its data. Use APIs for request and response, and SQS or EventBridge for asynchronous work.
Health checks, rolling or canary deploys, injected secrets, image scanning, and central logs and metrics.

why.reason: ECS for AWS-native simplicity; EKS when Kubernetes compatibility is required.
Fargate removes node work; EC2 can be cheaper at steady high utilization.
Decoupling stops one slow service from cascading into others.

scenarios.watch: Do not make a shared database the integration contract. Define timeouts, retries, idempotency, service ownership, and rollback.

scenarios.title: Disaster recovery
scenarios.scenario: Recover after an AZ or Region failure, within an agreed recovery point objective (RPO) and recovery time objective (RTO).

steps.text: Agree RTO (time to restore) and RPO (acceptable data loss) for each workload with the business.
Run the primary across AZs and protect data with backups and supported replication.
Keep the DR Region at the chosen readiness: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or active-active.
During an incident, check health and data consistency, promote dependencies, then switch traffic with the planned mechanism.
Test failover and failback regularly, including IAM, secrets, DNS, certificates, quotas, artifacts, and operator access.

why.reason: Lowest cost, longest recovery.
Faster recovery for more always-on cost.
Shortest recovery, highest complexity and data-consistency burden.

scenarios.watch: Replication copies corruption and deletes too. Pair it with protected point-in-time backups and a rehearsed runbook.

scenarios.title: Data lake and analytics
scenarios.scenario: Ingest batch and streaming data, catalog and transform it, query it cheaply, and publish trusted reporting datasets.

steps.text: Land immutable raw data in S3; streaming sources arrive through Kinesis Data Streams or Firehose.
Glue crawlers and ETL jobs build the catalog and curated datasets; the raw zone stays for replay and audit.
Parquet or ORC, compression, and partitions cut how many bytes Athena scans.
Athena handles ad hoc SQL; Redshift serves repeated warehouse workloads; QuickSight shows dashboards.
Lake Formation, IAM, and bucket policies govern access, with central audit logs.

why.reason: Athena for ad hoc SQL on lake files; Redshift for repeated, curated warehouse queries.
Keeps source fidelity while giving analysts consistent, fast datasets.
Catalog and transformation, not storage.

scenarios.watch: Data quality, schema evolution, PII controls, partition strategy, and ownership matter as much as the services.

scenarios.title: Asynchronous messaging and event processing
scenarios.scenario: Decouple producers from consumers, absorb bursts, retry failures safely, and broadcast events to independent systems.

steps.text: The producer emits an event; an EventBridge rule matches it and routes it on.
SNS fans out to several SQS queues, so each consumer has its own durable backlog.
Workers poll their queue; a failed message reappears after the visibility timeout and is retried.
After the maximum receive count, the message moves to the dead-letter queue for diagnosis and controlled redrive.
Handlers are idempotent; alarm on queue age, depth, delivery failures, and DLQ count.

why.reason: Durable pull-based queue that buffers bursts.
Fan-out with independent scaling and retries per consumer.
Rule-based routing, schedules, and many AWS targets.

scenarios.watch: Do not assume exactly-once processing. Design for duplicates, ordering limits, poison messages, and safe replay.

checklist.questions: Peak requests or events per second? Payload size? Latency target? Burst pattern? Global users?
Required uptime? Multi-AZ? Regional DR? Explicit RTO and RPO? Is failover tested?
Relational or key-value? Access patterns? Consistency? Retention? Backups and point-in-time recovery? Residency?
Who authenticates? Least-privilege roles? Private subnets? TLS and KMS? Secret rotation? Audit?
Synchronous API or asynchronous queue? Fan-out, ordering, replay, retries, DLQ?
Metrics, logs, traces, alarms, runbooks, rollback, infrastructure as code?
Always on or on demand? Data transfer? Storage tiers? Cache hit rate? Query scan cost?
What did you deliberately not choose, and why? What changes at 10 times the traffic?
